A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research on hallucinated targets, generate/pertask relabeling, and SSM/RDS experiments. Their readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial retitling and restructuring.

before.justification: V5 reports original controlled experiments with Skipper and LEAP on SSM and RDS, including estimation errors, behavior frequencies, and generalization performance over 20 seeds.

after.justification: V6 retains original Skipper/LEAP experiments and additionally reports Dyna/DynaX comparisons and non-singleton-target feasibility experiments.

M1.justification: V6 extends the proposal with an explicit feasibility evaluator using a TD hitting-time update, C51-style distributional outputs, and horizon-dependent rejection. Its DynaX adaptation suppresses infeasible simulated-transition updates. V5 primarily proposes relabeling and separate generator/estimator training while assuming suitable update rules; generate, pertask, and their mixture mechanisms are retained.

E1.justification: SSM and RDS remain the experimental environments. V6 additionally evaluates neighborhood targets containing up to five states, replacing exact-state completion in these added tests (Appendix G). This introduces a limited new goal specification and feasibility-evaluation scenario without expanding environmental domains.

E2.justification: V6 adds evaluated Dyna baselines against DynaX on SSM and RDS (Figures 4 and 16). Existing Skipper/LEAP relabeling comparator memberships remain after matching names such as F-E to E. Other planning methods listed in Table 2 are discussed applications, not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V6 adds background-planning evaluation using errors against optimal Q values, training-task success, and update-rejection rates. Its non-singleton tests use random-walk training data and modify both the termination indicator and ground-truth DP solver (Appendix G). These are substantial new evaluation designs; the original decision-time training budgets and OOD task sampling largely remain.

E4.justification: V6 adds controlled tests of whether feasibility estimation withstands non-singleton target semantics (Appendix G), while removing Skipper's detailed error decompositions for estimates originating from versus pointing toward G.1 states on both environments (v5 Figures 5 and 8). Generator-strategy and OOD-difficulty analyses are retained despite relocation.

E5.justification: V5 specifies 50% confidence intervals for the SSM behavior plots in Figure 3c/g and 95% elsewhere. V6 states that all presented intervals are 95% (Section 5). Both report 20 seeds; this changes stated uncertainty reporting without establishing additional runs.

E6.justification: V6 adds DynaX-versus-Dyna value-error, success, and rejection-rate results (Figures 4 and 16), plus non-singleton estimation results favoring E+P+G over E (Figures 17–18). Some retained curves are revised, including Skipper's SSM E.1 errors in Figure 3b. V5's directional E.1 breakdown results are removed.

T1.justification: V6 introduces formal set-valued targets, hitting times and tau-feasibility, a target-value decomposition (Equation 1), and Result 4.1 on removing infeasible members from target sets. The TD boundary conditions and distributional feasibility/discount construction add substantial mathematical development beyond v5's mostly conceptual treatment.

C1.justification: The central contribution broadens from diagnosing delusions and improving target-directed HER training to a general feasibility-based rejection mechanism for decision-time and background planning. V6's abstract and introduction claim a combined learning-rule, architecture, and relabeling solution applicable across three representative planning methods.

C2.justification: V6 develops applicability conditions involving state-set targets and the embedding/indicator functions, and explicitly leaves targets lacking the required state correspondence for future work. Non-singleton evidence is limited to estimation after inadequate control performance. Conversely, v5's explanation of the difficulty of learning estimates originating from hallucinated states is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix I.3 adds Dyna's equal-sized real/simulated minibatches and 0.05 rejection threshold, implemented by zeroing rejected-transition errors. Most Skipper/LEAP implementation details remain, but v5's explicit SSM maximum episode length of 128 is no longer stated. Both versions already provide the same code repository link.

R1.justification: V6 substantially expands positioning around background planning, generative-model hallucinations, distributional learning, and temporal abstraction, including Dyna, GSP, Dreamer, and MuZero. Several earlier HER-focused references disappear. V5's explicit explanation that generate adapts auxiliary training from Zhao et al. (2024) is also omitted from the corresponding strategy description.

P1.justification: The title changes, Romain Laroche joins the author list, and target-directed/estimator terminology becomes TAP/evaluator terminology. The introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten, experiments are reorganized, and the appendices are divided into three thematic parts.

P2.justification: V6 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws Figures 1–2, and redistributes v5 Figure 3 across main-text and appendix displays. It introduces target-categorization and method-application tables, adds Dyna and non-singleton plots, and removes the directional error-breakdown figures. These changes substantially alter visual organization.

improvement.justification: V6 addresses an important specification gap: v5 largely assumes suitable evaluator update rules, whereas v6 supplies an explicit feasibility-learning construction and tests rejection in Dyna. This strengthens methodological clarity and evidence for applicability beyond the original decision-time agents. Useful directional diagnostics are lost, and non-singleton experiments do not establish effective control, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in specification and empirical support.
